'''Kajkavian'''{{efn|Kajkavian is pronounced as {{IPAc-en|k|aɪ|ˈ|k|ɑː|v|i|ə|n}} and {{IPAc-en|k|aɪ|ˈ|k|æ|v|i|ə|n}} in English. The native Kajkavian words with which the speakers refer to it are the noun ''kajkavščina'' and the adjective ''kajkavski''. The [[Štokavian]] adjective for it is also ''kajkavski'', pronounced as {{IPA|sh|kǎjkaʋskiː|}},<ref>{{cite web | work = Hrvatski jezični portal | title = kàjkavskī | url=http://hjp.znanje.hr/index.php?show=search_by_id&id=el9hXxM%3D&keyword=kajkavski|access-date=21 March 2015}}</ref> whereas the noun for it is ''kajkavica'' or ''kajkavština'', the latter pronounced as {{IPA|sh|kajkǎːʋʃtina|}}<ref>{{cite web | work = Hrvatski jezični portal | title = kajkávština |url=http://hjp.znanje.hr/index.php?show=search_by_id&id=el9hXxU%3D&keyword=kajkav%C5%A1tina |access-date=21 March 2015}}</ref>}} is a [[South Slavic languages|South Slavic]] [[supradialect]] or [[language]] spoken primarily by [[Croats]] in much of [[Central Croatia]] and [[Gorski Kotar]].<ref name="Mattheier1991">{{Cite book |last=Klaus J. Mattheier |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4dccAQAAMAAJ |title=Sociolinguistica |publisher=M. Niemeyer |year=1991 |isbn=978-3-484-60368-4}}</ref><ref name="EliassonJahr1997">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YNDMzUXlSDkC&pg=PA29 |title=Language and Its Ecology: Essays in Memory of Einar Haugen |date=1997 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-014688-2 |editor-last=Eliasson |editor-first=Stig |pages=29– |language=en |editor-last2=Jahr |editor-first2=Ernst Håkon}}</ref>

It is part of the South Slavic [[dialect continuum]], being transitional to the supradialects of [[Čakavian]], [[Štokavian]] and the Slovene language.<ref name="Greenberg2008">{{Cite book |last=Greenberg |first=Marc L. |author1-link=Marc L. Greenberg |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wsxlAAAAMAAJ |title=A Short Reference Grammar of Slovene |publisher=Lincom Europa |year=2008 |isbn=978-3-89586-965-5 |language=en}}</ref> There are differing opinions over whether Kajkavian is best considered a dialect of the [[Serbo-Croatian]] language or a fully-fledged language of its own, as it is only partially mutually intelligible with either Čakavian or Štokavian and bears more similarities to [[Slovene language|Slovene]]; it is transitional to and fully [[Mutual intelligibility|mutually intelligible]] with [[Prekmurje Slovene]] and the dialects in Slovenian Lower Styria's region of [[Prlekija]] in terms of phonology and vocabulary.<ref name="Alexander2006">{{Cite book |last=Alexander |first=Ronelle |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6HTdZ5rxJ-cC&pg=PA388 |title=Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian, a Grammar: With Sociolinguistic Commentary |date=2006 |publisher=The University of Wisconsin Press |isbn=978-0-299-21193-6 |pages=388– |language=en}}</ref>

Outside Croatia's northernmost regions, Kajkavian is also spoken in [[Austria]]n [[Burgenland]] and a number of enclaves in [[Hungary]] along the Austrian and Croatian border and in [[Romania]].<ref name="GilbersNerbonne2000">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QqQgBVXp_H4C&pg=PA160 |title=Languages in Contact |date=2000 |publisher=Rodopi |isbn=90-420-1322-2 |editor-last=Gilbers |editor-first=Dicky |pages=160– |language=en |editor-last2=Nerbonne |editor-first2=John A. |editor-last3=Schaeken |editor-first3=J.}}</ref>

== Name ==
The term "Kajkavian" and the broader classification of what defines this dialect are relatively modern constructs. The dialect's name originates from the interrogative pronoun "kaj" ("what"). The names of the other supradialects of Serbo-Croatian also originate from their respective variants of the interrogative pronoun.<ref name="Comrie2009">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4DR-AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA331 |title=The World's Major Languages |date=2009 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-26156-7 |editor-last=Comrie |editor-first=Bernard |edition=2nd |pages=331– |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Kȁj |url=http://hjp.znanje.hr/index.php?show=search_by_id&id=el9hXRE%3D&keyword=kaj |access-date=6 May 2014 |work=Hrvatski jezični portal |publisher=Znanje d.d. and Srce |language=hr |archive-date=14 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414211923/http://hjp.znanje.hr/index.php?show=search_by_id&id=el9hXRE%3D&keyword=kaj |url-status=live }}</ref> The pronouns are just general indicators and not strict identifiers of the dialects. Some Kajkavian dialects use "ča" (common in [[Čakavian]]), while certain Čakavian dialects, like the [[Buzet dialect]] in [[Istria]], use "kaj". The names of these dialects are based on the most common pronoun used, not an absolute rule.

Autonyms used throughout history by various Kajkavian writers have been manifold, ranging from ''Slavic'' (''slavonski'', ''slovenski'', ''slovinski'') to ''Croatian'' (''horvatski'') or ''[[Illyrian (South Slavic)|Illyrian]]'' (''illirski'').<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zelić-Bučan |first=Benedikta |year=2000 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5bwhAQAAIAAJ |journal=Journal of Croatian Studies |doi=10.5840/jcroatstud2000414 |volume=41 |title=The National Name of the Croatian Language Throughout History |pages=56–112|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Svet med Muro in Dravo: Ob stoletnici 1. slovenskega tabora v Ljutomeru 1868–1968|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fTzRAAAAMAAJ|year=1968|publisher=Skupščina občine}}</ref> The naming went through several phases, with the Slavic-based name initially being dominant. Over time, the name ''Croatian'' started gaining ground mainly during the 17th century, and by the beginning of the 18th century, it had supplanted the older name ''Slavic''. The name also followed the same evolution in neighboring Slovene [[Prekmurje]] and some other border areas in what is now Slovenia, although there the name ''Slovene-Croatian'' (''slovensko-horvatski'') existed as well.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Golec |first=Boris |url=http://zimk.zrc-sazu.si/sites/default/files/ISBN9789619219812.pdf |title=Hrvaški etnonim in lingvonim na Slovenskem v 17. in 18. stoletju s posebnim ozirom na Prekmurje |page=259 |language=sl |trans-title=The Croatian ethnonym and linguonym in Slovene lands during 17th and 18th century with special focus on Prekmurje |access-date=13 March 2015 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402112324/http://zimk.zrc-sazu.si/sites/default/files/ISBN9789619219812.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The actual term Kajkavian (''kajkavski''), including as an adjective, was invented in the 19th century and is credited to Serbian philologist [[Đuro Daničić]], while it was generally used and promoted in the 20th century works by Croatian writer [[Miroslav Krleža]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://jezik.hr/zaseban-jezik.html |title=Hrvatski – Zaseban jezik |website=jezik.hr |publisher=[[Institute of Croatian Language and Linguistics]] |access-date=8 April 2023 |quote=Pridjev kajkavski po podatcima iz Akademijina rječnika prvi je upotrijebio Đuro Daničić, a u Habdelićevu i Belostenčevu rječniku nije naveden. U Rječniku hrvatskoga kajkavskog književnog jezika potvrde za pridjev kajkavski nalazimo tek u Krležinim djelima. Kajkavska gramatika Ignaca Kristijanovića naziva se Grammatik der Kroatischen Mundart (1837.), iz čega je razvidno kako je i taj autor materinsko narječje nazivao hrvatskim imenom.}}</ref> The term is today accepted by its speakers in Croatia.

In English, Kajkavian is sometimes spelled as ''Kaykavian'', ''Kaikavian'' or ''Caicavian''.

== Classification ==
Historically, the [[Language classification|classification]] of Kajkavian has been a subject of much debate regarding both the question of whether it ought to be considered a dialect or a language, as well as the question of what its relation is to neighboring vernaculars.

The problem with classifying Kajkavian within South Slavic stems in part from its both structural differences and closesness with neighboring Čakavian and Štokavian speeches as well as its historical closeness to Slovene speeches. Some [[Slavist]]s maintain that when the separation of [[Western South Slavic]] speeches happened, they separated into five divergent groups — Slovene, Kajkavian, Čakavian, Western Štokavian and Eastern Štokavian, as a result of this, throughout history Kajkavian has often been categorized differently, either a node categorized together with Serbo-Croatian or Slovene.<ref name="Matasović 2008 66">{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p=66|ps=:Moguš (1971: 23 i dalje) slijedi Junkovića (disertacija iz 1967., objavljena 1972) u pobijanju Ramovševih (1936) izoglosa kojima se kajkavski genetskolingvistički pripisuje slovenskomu jeziku. Premda nije posve eksplicitan, i on, čini se, vjeruje u genetsko jedinstvo čakavskoga, kajkavskoga i štokavskoga. M. Lončarić (2005: 46) dopušta mogučnost da se iz zapadnojužnoslavenskoga izdvojilo pet primarnih odvjetaka: slovenski, kajkavski, čakavski, šćakavski (zapadnoštokavski) i (istočno-)štokavski, što je u osnovi i naša teza.}}</ref><ref name="Kapovic 4445" /> Furthermore, there do exist few old isoglosses that separate almost all Slovene speeches from all other Western South Slavic dialects, and do exist innovations exist common to Kajkavian, Čakavian, and Western Štokavian that would separate them from Slovene.<ref name="Mijo">{{cite journal |last=Lončarić |first=Mijo |date=1988 |title=Rani razvitak kajkavštine |trans-title=Early development of Kajkavian |url=https://hrcak.srce.hr/69872 |language=hr |journal=Rasprave |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=92–99 |access-date=12 February 2023}}</ref><ref name="Matasović 2008 65">{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p=65}}</ref><ref name="BirnbaumPuhvel1966">{{cite book
|author1=Henrik Birnbaum|author2=Jaan Puhvel
|title=Ancient Indo-European Dialects: Proceedings of the Conference on Indo-European Linguistics Held at the University of California, Los Angeles, April 25-27, 1963
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5pCBRsfJMv8C&pg=PA188
|year=1966|publisher=University of California Press
|pages=188–
|id=GGKEY:JUG4225Y4H2
}}</ref> Croatian linguist Stjepan Ivšić has used Kajkavian vocabulary and accentuation, which significantly differs from that of Štokavian, as evidence to be a language in its own right.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ivšić |first=Stjepan |title=Jezik Hrvata kajkavaca |date=1996 |publisher=Matica hrvatska |editor-last=Lisac |editor-first=Josip |edition=New |location=Zaprešić |language=hr |trans-title=The Language of the Kajkavian Croats}}</ref> Josip Silić, one of the main initiators behind the standardisation of Croatian, also regards Kajkavian as a distinct language by dint of its having significantly different morphology, syntax and phonology from the official Štokavian-based standard.<ref>Silić, Josip (1998), Hrvatski standardni jezik i hrvatska narječja, Kolo. 8, 4, p. 425-430.</ref> However, Silić's theorization about three languages and systems of Croatian, based on [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] and [[Eugenio Coșeriu]] concepts, is criticized for being exaggerated, incomprehensible and logically non-existent.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ivašković |first=Igor |date=2020 |title=Razlikovanje jezika u hrvatskom jezikoslovlju u svjetlu de Saussureove strukturalističke teorije |trans-title=Language Differentiation in Croatian Linguistics in the Light of de Saussure's Structuralist Theory |url=https://hrcak.srce.hr/243215 |language=hr |journal=Jezik |volume=67 |issue=2–3 |pages=62–67, 69}}</ref> According to [[Ranko Matasović]], Kajkavian is equally Croatian as Čakavian and Štokavian dialects.<ref name="Matasović 2008 67">{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p=67}}</ref> [[Mate Kapović]] notes that the dialects are practical and provisory linguistic inventions which should not be misunderstood and extrapolated outside the context of the [[dialect continuum]].<ref name="Kapovic 2015 9106366">{{harvnb|Kapović|2015|pp=9–10, 63–66}}</ref>

According to [[Mijo Lončarić]] (1988), the formation of the Proto-Kajkavian linguistic and territorial unit would be around the 10th century (when it separated from Southwestern Slavic), until the 12th century it is a separate node of Croatian-Serbian language family (excluding Slovene), between the 13th and 15th century when formed as a dialect with main features known today, until the end of the 17th century when lost a part of spoken territory (to the South, Southeast and especially to East in Slavonia), and from the 17th-18th century till present time when regained part of lost territory by forming new transitional dialects.<ref name="Mijo" />

== Characteristics ==
[[File:Serbo croatian dialects historical distribution 2.png|thumb|Distribution of Čakavian, Kajkavian and Western Štokavian before 16th century migrations. Kajkavian in yellow.]]
[[File:Croatian dialects in Cro and BiH 1.PNG|thumb|Location map of Serbo-Croatian dialects in Croatia and areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina with Croatian majority. Kajkavian in purple.]]
The Kajkavian speech area borders in the northwest on the [[Slovene language]] and in the northeast on the [[Hungarian language]]. In the east and southeast it is bordered by Štokavian dialects roughly along a line that used to serve as the border between [[Civil Croatia]] and the [[Habsburg]] [[Military Frontier]]. Finally, in the southwest, it borders Čakavian along the Kupa and Dobra rivers.<ref name="Stepanović1986">{{cite book|author= Predrag Stepanović|title= A Taxonomic Description of the Dialects of Serbs and Croats in Hungary: The Štokavian Dialect|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=irNiAAAAMAAJ|year= 1986|publisher= Akad. K.|isbn= 978-3-412-07484-5}}</ref> It is thought by M. Lončarić that historically these borders extended further to the south and east, for example, the eastern border is thought to have extended at least well into modern-day [[Slavonia]] to the area around the town of [[Pakrac]] and [[Slatina, Croatia|Slatina]], while East of it transitional Kajkavian-[[Slavonian dialect|Štokavian dialects]].<ref name="Matasovic 35">{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p=35}}</ref> The transitional dialects during Ottoman invasion and migrations almost completely vanished.<ref name="Kapovic 4445">{{harvnb|Kapović|2015|pp=44–45}}</ref>

The Croatian capital, [[Zagreb]], has historically been a Kajkavian-speaking area, and Kajkavian is still in use by its older and (to a lesser extent) by its younger population. Modern Zagreb speech has come under considerable influence from Štokavian.<ref>{{cite journal |url= http://www.matica.hr/kolo/301/Najnovije%20jezi%C4%8Dne%20promjene%20u%20zagreba%C4%8Dkom%20govoru/ |title= Najnovije jezične promjene u zagrebačkom govoru |first= Mate |last= Kapović |year= 2006 |journal= Kolo |volume= 4 |language= hr |archive-date= 2014-03-06 |access-date= 2014-02-28 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140306121233/http://www.matica.hr/kolo/301/Najnovije%20jezi%C4%8Dne%20promjene%20u%20zagreba%C4%8Dkom%20govoru/ |url-status= live }}</ref> The vast intermingling of Kajkavian and standard Štokavian in Zagreb and its surroundings has led to problems in defining the underlying structure of those speech-groups. As a result, many of the urban speeches (but not rural ones) have been labelled either ''Kajkavian [[Koiné language|koine]]'' or ''Kajkavian–Štokavian'' rather than Kajkavian or Štokavian.<ref name="PützDirven1996">{{cite book|author1= Martin Pütz|author2= René Dirven|title= The Construal of Space in Language and Thought|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=YvjIgwzkevEC&pg=PA50|date= 1 January 1996|publisher= Walter de Gruyter|isbn= 978-3-11-015243-2|pages= 50– }}</ref> Additionally, the forms of speech in use exhibit significant sociolinguistic variation. Research suggests that younger Zagreb-born speakers of the Kajkavian koine tend to consciously use more Kajkavian features when speaking to older people, showing that such features are still in their linguistic inventory even if not used at all times.<ref name="StephanyVoeikova2009">{{cite book|author1= Ursula Stephany|author2= Maria D. Voeikova|title= Development of Nominal Inflection in First Language Acquisition: A Cross-Linguistic Perspective|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=kCRfiaMCFsMC&pg=PA158|date= 14 July 2009|publisher= Walter de Gruyter|isbn= 978-3-11-021711-7|pages= 158–}}</ref> However, the Kajkavian koine is distinct from Kajkavian as spoken in non-urban areas, and the mixing of Štokavian and Kajkavian outside of urban settings is much rarer and less developed. The Kajkavian koine has also been named ''Zagreb Štokavian'' by some{{which|date=April 2018}}.<ref name="PützDirven1996" />

As a result of the previously mentioned mixing of dialects, various Kajkavian features and characteristics have found their way into the standard Štokavian (''standard Croatian'') spoken in those areas. For example, some of the prominent features are the fixed stress-based accentual system without distinctive lengths, the merger of /č/ and /ć/ and of /dž/ and /đ/, vocabulary differences as well as a different place of stress in words.<ref>{{citation |first= Mate |last= Kapović |title= Jezični utjecaj velikih gradova |language=hr |url= http://hrcak.srce.hr/file/14526 |format= PDF |year= 2004 |journal= Rasprave Instituta Za Hrvatski Jezik I Jezikoslovlje |volume= 30 }}</ref> The Zagreb variety of Štokavian is considered by some to enjoy parallel prestige with the prescribed Štokavian variety. Because of that, speakers whose native speech is closer to the standard variety often end up adopting the Zagreb speech for various reasons.<ref name="kapovic001">{{citation |first= Mate |last= Kapović |title= Čiji je jezik? |trans-title= Who does language belong to? |language= hr |url= https://bib.irb.hr/datoteka/503036.Kapovic_Ciji_je_jezik.pdf |year= 2010 |pages= 67– |access-date= 2015-03-29 |archive-date= 2020-01-15 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200115203909/https://bib.irb.hr/datoteka/503036.Kapovic_Ciji_je_jezik.pdf |url-status= dead }}</ref>

Kajkavian is closely related to Slovene – and to [[Prekmurje Slovene]] in particular.<ref>{{cite book|title= Časopis za zgodovino in narodopisje: Review for history and ethnography|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=rNoVAQAAMAAJ|year= 1988|publisher= Univerza v Mariboru in Zgodovinsko društvo Maribor}}</ref> Higher amounts of correspondences between the two exist in inflection and vocabulary. The speakers of the Prekmurje dialect are [[Slovenes]] and [[Hungarian Slovenes]] who belonged to the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Zagreb|Archdiocese of Zagreb]] during the Habsburg era (until 1918). They used Kajkavian as their liturgical language, and by the 18th century, Kajkavian had become the standard language of Prekmurje.<ref name="Golec2012">{{cite book|author= Boris Golec|title= Nedokončana kroatizacija delov vzhodne Slovenije med 16. in 19. stoletjem: po sledeh hrvaškega lingvonima in etnonima v Beli krajini, Kostelu, Prekmurju in Prlekiji|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=92S7E1MPBy0C&pg=PA170|year= 2012|publisher= Založba ZRC|isbn= 978-961-254-383-9|pages= 170–}}</ref> Moreover, literary Kajkavian was also used in neighboring [[Styria (Slovenia)|Slovene Styria]] during the 17th and 18th centuries, and in parts of it, education was conducted in Kajkavian.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.ung.si/~library/diplome/SLOVENISTIKA/33Vekjet.pdf |title= Slovenski jezik v šolstvu: Slovenščina kot učni jezik v času razsvetljenstva |trans-title= Slovene language in education: Slovene as a language of instruction during the Enlightenment |pages= 64–65 |language= sl|access-date= 12 March 2015 |author= Ivana Vekjet Frančeškin |publisher= [[University of Nova Gorica]]}}</ref>

As a result of various factors, Kajkavian has numerous differences compared to Štokavian:

* Kajkavian has a prothetic ''v-'' generalized in front of ''u'' (compare Kajkavian ''vuho'', Štokavian ''uho''; Kajkavian ''vugel'', Štokavian ''ugao''; Kajkavian ''vučil'', Štokavian ''učio''). This feature has been attested in Glagolitic texts very early on, already around the 15th century (Petrisov zbornik, 1468). A similar feature exists in [[Common Czech|colloquial Czech]],<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 140}}</ref> as well as in many [[Slovene dialects]], especially from the [[Pannonian dialect group|Pannonian]], [[Styrian dialect group|Styrian]] and [[Littoral dialect group]]s.
* Proto-Slavic *dj resulted in Kajkavian ''j'' as opposed to Štokavian ''đ'' (cf. Kajkavian ''meja'', Štokavian ''međa'', Slovene ''meja'').<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p=148}}</ref>
* The nasal *ǫ has evolved into a closed /o/ in Kajkavian (cf. Kajkavian ''roka'', Štokavian ''ruka'', Slovene ''roka'').<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 152}}</ref>
* Common Slavic *v and *v- survived as ''v'' in Kajkavian, whereas in Štokavian they resulted in ''u'' and ''u-'', and in Čakavian they gave way to ''va''.<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 157}}</ref> The same feature is maintained in most Slovene dialects.
* Kajkavian has retained /č/ in front of /r/ (cf. Kajkavian ''črn'', ''črv'', Štokavian ''crn'', ''crv'', Slovene ''črn'', ''črv'').<ref name="Matasović 2008 161">{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 161}}</ref>
* Kajkavian /ž/ in front of a vowel turns into /r/. A similar evolution happened in Slovene, Čakavian as well as Western Štokavian, however the latter does not use it in its standard form (cf. Kajkavian ''moči > morem/moreš/more'', Štokavian ''moći > mogu/možeš/može'', Slovene ''moči > morem/moreš/more'').<ref name="Matasović 2008 161" />
* Kajkavian retains ''-jt'' and ''-jd'' clusters (cf. Kajkavian ''pojti'', ''pojdem'', Štokavian ''poći'', ''pođem'').<ref name="Matasović 2008 161" /> This feature is shared by standard Slovene.
* Like most Slavic varieties (including Slovenian, but not Štokavian), Kajkavian exhibits [[final-obstruent devoicing]], however it is not consistently spelled out (cf. Kajkavian ''vrak'', Štokavian ''vrag'')<ref>{{cite book|title= International Review of Slavic Linguistics|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=hI7jAAAAMAAJ|year= 1982|publisher= Linguistic Research|isbn = 978-0-88783-046-4}}</ref>
* Diminutive suffixes in Kajkavian are ''-ek'', ''-ec'', ''-eko'', ''-eco'' (cf. Kajkavian ''pes > pesek'', Štokavian ''pas > psić'').<ref name="Savickien?Dressler2007">{{cite book|author1= Ineta Savickien?|author2= Wolfgang U. Dressler|title= The Acquisition of Diminutives: A Cross-linguistic Perspective|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=VoDKM0hvVKUC&pg=PA76|date= 1 January 2007|publisher= John Benjamins Publishing|isbn= 978-90-272-5303-3|pages= 76–}}</ref> The same diminutive suffixes are found in Slovene.
* Negative past-tense construction in Kajkavian deviates syntactically from neighboring speeches in its placing of the negative particle. Some argued that this might indicate a remnant of the Pannonian Slavic system. Similar behavior occurs in Slovak (compare Kajkavian ''ja sem nę čul'', Slovene ''jaz nisem čul'', Štokavian ''ja nisam čuo'').<ref name="Nuorluoto 2010 42">{{harvnb|Nuorluoto|2010|p=42}}</ref>
* Some variants of Kajkavian have a different first-person plural present-tense suffix, ''-mę'' (cf. Kajkavian ''-mę'', ''rečemę'', Slovene ''-mo'', ''rečemo'', Štokavian ''-mo'', ''kažemo'', Slovak ''-me'', ''povieme'') such as the Bednja dialect, although most Kajkavian sub-dialects retain the suffix ''-mo.''<ref>{{harvnb|Nuorluoto|2010|p= 41}}</ref>
* Relative pronouns differ from neighboring dialects and languages (although they are similar to Slovene). Kajkavian uses ''kateri'', ''tęri'' and ''šteri'' depending on sub-dialect (cf. Czech ''který'', Slovak ''ktorý'', Štokavian ''koji'', standard Slovene ''kateri'', [[Carniola]]n dialects ''k'teri'', ''kęri'').<ref name="Nuorluoto 2010 42" />
* The genitive plural in Štokavian adds an -a to the end, whereas Kajkavian retains the old form (cf. Kajkavian ''vuk'', ''vukov/vukof'', Štokavian ''vuk'', ''vukova'', Slovene ''volk'', ''volkov'', Kajkavian ''žene'', ''žen'', Štokavian ''žene'', ''žena'', Slovene ''žene'', ''žen''/''žena'').<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 186}}</ref>
* Kajkavian retains the older locative plural (compare Kajkavian ''prsti'', ''prsteh'', Štokavian ''prsti'', ''prstima'', Slovene ''prsti'', ''prstih'').<ref name="Matasović 2008 187">{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 187}}</ref>
* The loss of the [[Dual (grammatical number)|dual]] is considered to be significantly more recent than in Štokavian.<ref name="Matasović 2008 187" />
* Kajkavian has no vocative case.<ref name="Matasović 2008 187" /> This feature is shared with standard Slovene and most Slovene dialects.
* So-called ''s-type nouns'' have been retained as a separate declension class in Kajkavian contrasted from the neuter due to the formant ''-es-'' in oblique cases. The same is true for Slovene (compare Kajkavian ''čudo'', ''čudesa'', Štokavian ''čudo'', ''čuda'', Slovene ''čudo'', ''čudesa'').<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|pp= 205–206}}</ref>
* Kajkavian has no [[aorist]].<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 269}}</ref> The same is true for Slovene.
* The [[supine]] has been retained as distinctive from infinitive, as in Slovene. The infinitive suffixes are ''-ti'', ''-či'' whereas their supine counterparts are ''-t'', ''-č''. The supine and the infinitive are often stressed differently. The supine is used with verbs of motion.<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 301}}</ref>
* The future tense is formed with the auxiliary ''biti'' and the ''-l'' participle as in standard Slovene and similar to Czech and Slovak (compare Kajkavian ''išel bom'', Štokavian ''ići ću'', standard Slovene ''šel bom'', eastern Slovene dialects ''išel bom'').<ref name="Nuorluoto 2010 42" />
* Modern urban Kajkavian speeches tend to have stress as the only significant prosodic feature as opposed to the Štokavian four-tone system.<ref name="Magner1966">{{cite book|author= Thomas F. Magner|title= A Zagreb Kajkavian Dialect|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=IDE-AAAAIAAJ|year= 1966|publisher= Pennsylvania State University}}</ref>
* Kajkavian exhibits various syntactic influences from German.<ref name="Reindl2008">{{cite book|author= Donald F. Reindl|title= Language Contact, German and Slovenian|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=vdaHGTDi9s8C&pg=PA96|year= 2008|publisher= Brockmeyer Verlag|isbn= 978-3-8196-0715-8|pages= 96–}}</ref>
* The Slavic prefix u- has a ''vi-'' reflex in some dialects, similar to Czech ''vý-'' (compare Kajkavian ''vigled'', Czech ''výhled'', Štokavian ''izgled'').<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p= 37}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last= Bjeletić|first= Marta|title= Praslovenska leksika u etimološkom rečniku srpskohrvatskog jezika|url= http://elibrary.matf.bg.ac.rs/bitstream/handle/123456789/1022/MartaBjeleticPraslovenskaLeksikaUEtimoloskomRecnikuSprskohrvatskogJezika.pdf|work= Praslowianszczyzna i jej rozpad|year= 1998|access-date= 10 March 2015|archive-date= 28 April 2015|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150428191215/http://elibrary.matf.bg.ac.rs/bitstream/handle/123456789/1022/MartaBjeleticPraslovenskaLeksikaUEtimoloskomRecnikuSprskohrvatskogJezika.pdf|url-status= live}}</ref> This feature sets Kajkavian apart from Slovene, which shares the prefix -iz with Štokavian.

In addition to the above list of characteristics that set Kajkavian apart from Štokavian, research suggests possible a closer relation with Kajkavian and the [[Slovak language]], especially with the Central Slovak dialects upon which standard Slovak is based. As modern-day Hungary used to be populated by Slavic-speaking peoples prior to the arrival of Hungarians, there have been hypotheses on possible common innovations of future West and South Slavic speakers of that area. Kajkavian is the most prominent of the South Slavic speeches in sharing the most features that could potentially be common [[Pannonian Basin|Pannonian]] innovations.<ref>{{harvnb|Nuorluoto|2010|pp= 37}}</ref>

Some Kajkavian words bear a closer resemblance to other Slavic languages such as [[Russian language|Russian]] than they do to Štokavian or Čakavian. For instance ''gda'' (also seen as shorter "da") seems to be at first glance unrelated to ''kada'', however when compared to Russian ''когда'', Slovene ''kdaj'', or Prekmurje Slovene ''gda'', ''kda'', the relationship becomes apparent. Kajkavian ''kak'' (''how'') and ''tak'' (''so'') are exactly like their Russian cognates and Prekmurje Slovene compared to Štokavian, Čakavian, and standard Slovene ''kako'' and ''tako''. (This vowel loss occurred in most other Slavic languages; Štokavian is a notable exception, whereas the same feature in [[Macedonian language|Macedonian]] is probably not due to Serbo-Croatian influence because the word is preserved in the same form in [[Bulgarian language|Bulgarian]], to which Macedonian is much more closely related than to Serbo-Croatian).<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Levinson|O'Leary|1992|p= 239}}</ref>

==Phonology==
The number of vowels and consonants can vary by region, but the typical Kajkavian phoneme set includes 7 vowels and 23 consonants.<ref>Mijo Lončarić: ''Kajkavsko narječje'', Školska knjiga, Zagreb 1996.</ref><ref>Dalibor Brozović, ''Jezik, srpskohrvatski/hrvatskosrpski, hrvatski ili srpski'', Jugoslavenski leksikografski zavod "Miroslav Krleža", Zagreb, 1988.</ref>

In most cases, voiced consonants are devoiced at the end of words, unless followed by a word beginning with a vowel or voiced consonant. For example, the words ''grob'' (grave), ''poleg'' (next to, alongside) and ''njegov'' (his) become ''grop'', ''polek'' and ''njegof'' respectively.

==History of research==
Linguistic investigation began during the 19th century, although the research itself often ended in non-linguistic or outdated conclusions. Since that was the age of national revivals across Europe as well as the South Slavic lands, the research was steered by national narratives. Within that framework, Slovene philologists such as [[Franz Miklosich]] and [[Jernej Kopitar]] attempted to reinforce the idea of Slovene and Kajkavian unity and asserted that Kajkavian speakers are Slovenes.<ref name="Lončarić 1985 284">{{harvnb|Lončarić|1985|p=284}}</ref> On the other hand, [[Josef Dobrovský]] also claimed linguistic and national unity between the two groups but under the Croatian ethnonym.<ref name="Lončarić 1985 284" /><ref name="TrencsényiKopeček2006">{{cite book|author1=Balázs Trencsényi|author2=Michal Kopeček|title=Late Enlightenment: Emergence of Modern National Ideas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k5Vsjg508EYC&pg=PA226|year=2006|publisher=Central European University Press|isbn=978-963-7326-52-3|pages=226–}}</ref>

The first modern dialectal investigations of Kajkavian started at the end of the 19th century. The Ukrainian philologist A. M. Lukjanenko wrote the first comprehensive monograph on Kajkavian (titled ''Кайкавское нарѣчiе'' (''Kajkavskoe narečie'') meaning ''The Kajkavian dialect'') in Russian in 1905.<ref>{{harvnb|Lončarić|1985|p=281}}</ref> Kajkavian dialects have been classified along various criteria: for instance Serbian philologist [[Aleksandar Belić]] divided (1927) the Kajkavian dialect according to the reflexes of Proto-Slavic phonemes /tj/ and /dj/ into three subdialects: eastern, northwestern and southwestern.<ref>{{harvnb|Lončarić|1985|p=288}}</ref>

However, later investigations did not corroborate Belić's division. Contemporary Kajkavian dialectology begins with Croatian philologist [[Stjepan Ivšić]]'s work "Jezik Hrvata kajkavaca" (''The Language of Kajkavian Croats'', 1936), which highlighted accentual characteristics. Due to the great diversity within Kajkavian primarily in phonetics, phonology, and morphology, the Kajkavian dialect atlas features a large number of subdialects: from four identified by Ivšić to six proposed by Croatian linguist [[Dalibor Brozović|Brozović]] (formerly the accepted division) all the way up to fifteen according to a monograph by Croatian linguist [[Mijo Lončarić]] (1995). The traditional division in six sub-dialects includes: ''zagorsko-međimurski'', ''križevačko-podravski'', ''turopoljsko-posavski'', ''prigorski'' (transitional to [[Central Čakavian]]), ''donjosutlanski'' (migratory transitional Čakavian-ikavian which became Kajkavian), and ''goranski'' (also transitional which is more Kajkavian in lesser Eastern part, while more Slovene in main Western part).<ref name="Kapovic 4445" /> Kajkavian categorization of transitional dialects, like for example of ''prigorski'', is provisory.<ref name="Kapovic 63">{{harvnb|Kapović|2015|p=63}}</ref>

== Area of use ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=January 2026}}[[File:Kamenita vulicza.jpg|thumb|Bilingual Kajkavian/German street sign in [[Zagreb]]:<br />Kamenita Vulicza / Stein Gasse]]
Kajkavian is mainly spoken in northern and northwestern Croatia. The mixed half-Kajkavian towns along the eastern and southern edge of the Kajkavian-speaking area are [[Pitomača]], [[Čazma]], [[Kutina]], [[Popovača]], [[Sunja, Sisak-Moslavina County|Sunja]], [[Petrinja]], [[Martinska Ves, Sisak-Moslavina County|Martinska Ves]], [[Ozalj]], [[Ogulin]], [[Fužine, Croatia|Fužine]], and [[Čabar]], including newer Štokavian enclaves of [[Bjelovar]], [[Sisak]], [[Glina, Croatia|Glina]], [[Donja Dubrava, Zagreb|Donja Dubrava]] and [[Novi Zagreb]]. The southernmost Kajkavian villages are [[Krapje, Croatia|Krapje]] at [[Jasenovac, Sisak-Moslavina County|Jasenovac]]; and [[Pavušek]], [[Dvorišče]] and [[Hrvatsko selo]] in Zrinska Gora (R. Fureš & A. Jembrih: ''Kajkavski u povijesnom i sadašnjem obzorju'' p. 548, Zabok 2006).

The major cities in northern Croatia are located in what was historically a Kajkavian-speaking area, mainly Zagreb, Koprivnica, Krapina, Križevci, Varaždin, Čakovec. The typical archaic Kajkavian is today spoken mainly in [[Hrvatsko Zagorje]] hills and [[Međimurje County|Međimurje]] plain, and in adjacent areas of northwestern Croatia where immigrants and the Štokavian standard had much less influence. Many of northern Croatian urban areas today are partly Štokavianized due to the influence of the [[standard language]] and immigration of Štokavian speakers. Other southeastern people who immigrate to Zagreb from Štokavian territories often pick up rare elements of Kajkavian in order to assimilate, notably the pronoun "kaj" instead of "što" and the extended use of future anterior (''futur drugi''), but they never adapt well because of alien eastern accents and ignoring Kajkavian-Čakavian archaisms and syntax.

=== Bednja variant ===
The most peculiar Kajkavian dialect ''(Bednjounski)'' is spoken in [[Bednja, Varaždin County|Bednja]] in northernmost Croatia.

== Literary Kajkavian ==
[[File:Danica zagrebecka (1850).jpg|thumb|A picture of the 1850 edition of the Kajkavian periodical ''Danica zagrebečka'']]
Writings that are judged by some as being distinctly Kajkavian can be dated to around the 12th century.<ref>{{harvnb|Matasović|2008|p=36}}</ref> The first comprehensive works in Kajkavian started to appear during the 16th century at a time when Central Croatia gained prominence due to the geopolitical environment since it was free from Ottoman occupation. The most notable work of that era was [[Ivanuš Pergošić]]'s {{lang|la|Decretum}}, released in 1574. {{lang|la|Decretum}} was a translation of [[István Werbőczy]]'s {{lang|la|[[Tripartitum]]}}.

At the same time, many Protestant writers of the Slovene lands also released their works in Kajkavian in order to reach a wider audience, while also using some Kajkavian features in their native writings. During that time, the autonym used by the writers was usually {{lang|kjv|slovinski}} (Slavic), {{lang|kjv|horvatski}} (Croatian) or {{lang|kjv|ilirski}} (Illyrian).<ref>{{harvnb|Lončarić|1985|p=282}}</ref>

After that, numerous works appeared in the Kajkavian literary language: chronicles by [[Antun Vramec|Vramec]], liturgical works by [[Juraj Ratkaj|Ratkaj]], [[Juraj Habdelić|Habdelić]], [[Juraj Mulih|Mulih]]; poetry by [[Ana Katarina Zrinska]] and [[Fran Krsto Frankopan]], and a dramatic opus by [[Tituš Brezovački]]. Kajkavian-based are important lexicographic works like [[Andrija Jambrešić|Jambrešić]]'s "{{lang|kjv|Dictionar}}", 1670, and the monumental (2,000 pages and 50,000 words) Latin-Kajkavian-Latin dictionary "{{lang|la|Gazophylacium}}" (including also some Čakavian and Štokavian words marked as such) by [[Ivan Belostenec]] (posthumously, 1740). [[Miroslav Krleža]]'s poetic work "{{lang|kjv|[[Balade Petrice Kerempuha]]}}" drew heavily on Belostenec's dictionary. Kajkavian grammars include [[Franz Kornig|Kornig]]'s, 1795, [[Josip Matijević|Matijević]]'s, 1810 and [[Josip Đurkovečki|Đurkovečki]]'s, 1837.

During that time, the Kajkavian literary language was the dominant written form in its spoken area along with Latin and German.<ref>{{harvnb|Lončarić|1985|p=285}}</ref> Until [[Ljudevit Gaj]]'s attempts to modernize the spelling, Kajkavian was written using [[Hungarian orthography|Hungarian spelling conventions]].<ref name="FishmanGarcia2011a">{{cite book|author1=Joshua Fishman|author2=Ofelia Garcia|title=Handbook of Language and Ethnic Identity: The Success-Failure Continuum in Language and Ethnic Identity Efforts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oUydX_3rG0AC&pg=PA367|date=16 March 2011|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-983799-1|pages=367–}}</ref> Kajkavian began to lose its status during the [[Croatian National Revival]] in mid-19th Century when the leaders of the [[Illyrian movement]] opted to use the Štokavian dialect as the basis for the future South Slavic standard language, the reason being that it had the highest number of speakers. Initially, the choice of Štokavian was accepted even among Slovene intellectuals, but later it fell out of favor.<ref name="FishmanGarcia2011b">{{cite book|author1=Joshua Fishman|author2=Ofelia Garcia|title=Handbook of Language and Ethnic Identity: The Success-Failure Continuum in Language and Ethnic Identity Efforts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oUydX_3rG0AC&pg=PA372|date=16 March 2011|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-983799-1|pages=372–}}</ref> The Zagreb linguistic school was opposed to the course that the standardization process took. Namely, it had almost completely ignored Kajkavian (and Čakavian) dialects which was contrary to the original vision of Zagreb school. With the notable exception of vocabulary influence of Kajkavian on the standard Croatian register (but not the Serbian one), there was very little to no input from other non-Štokavian dialects.<ref name="Greenberg2004">{{cite book|author=Robert D. Greenberg|title=Language and Identity in the Balkans: Serbo-Croatian and Its Disintegration|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_lNjHgr3QioC&pg=PA28|date=25 March 2004|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-151455-5|pages=28–}}</ref> Instead, the opposite was done, with some modern-day linguists calling the process of 19th-century standardization an event of "neo-Štokavian purism" and a "purge of non-Štokavian elements".<ref name="kapovic001" />

Early 20th century witnessed a drastic increase in released Kajkavian literature, although by then it had become part of what was considered Croatian dialectal poetry with no pretense of serving as a standard written form. The most notable writers of this period were among others, [[Antun Gustav Matoš]], [[Miroslav Krleža]], [[Ivan Goran Kovačić]], [[Dragutin Domjanić]] and [[Nikola Pavić]].

Kajkavian lexical treasure is being published by the [[Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts]] in {{lang|kjv|Rječnik hrvatskoga kajkavskoga književnoga jezika}} ("Dictionary of the Croatian Kajkavian Literary Language", 8 volumes, 1999).

Later, [[Dario Vid Balog]], actor, linguist and writer translated the New Testament in Kajkavian.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.me.com/jurek/kajkavski/matej.html|title=iCloud|work=me.com|access-date=25 February 2015|archive-date=20 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110820074119/http://web.me.com/jurek/kajkavski/matej.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2018 is published the Kajkavian translation of [[Antoine de Saint-Exupéry]]'s ''[[The Little Prince]]'' ({{lang|fr|Le Petit Prince}}) by [[Kajkavsko spravišče]] aka {{lang|kjv|Mali kralevič}}.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bozicabrkan.com/mali-princ-je-pregovoril-kajkavski-umjesto-kave-15-prosinca-2018/ |title=Mali Princ je pregovoril kajkavski! – Umjesto kave 15. prosinca 2018. (bozicabrkan.com) |access-date=2018-12-22 |archive-date=2018-12-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181223073628/http://www.bozicabrkan.com/mali-princ-je-pregovoril-kajkavski-umjesto-kave-15-prosinca-2018/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Kajkavian media ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=January 2025}}
During [[Yugoslavia]] in the 20th century, Kajkavian was mostly restricted to private communication, poetry and folklore.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}} With the recent regional democratizing and cultural revival beginning in the 1990s, Kajkavian partly regained its former half-public position chiefly in Zagorje and Varaždin Counties and local towns, where there is now some public media e.g.:
* A quarterly periodical ''"Kaj"'', with 35 annual volumes in nearly a hundred fascicles published since 1967 by the Kajkavian Association ('Kajkavsko Spravišče') in Zagreb.
* An autumnal week of ''Kajkavian culture'' in Krapina since 1997, with professional symposia on Kajkavian resulting in five published proceedings.
* An annual periodical, ''Hrvatski sjever'' ('Croatian North'), with a dozen volumes partly in Kajkavian published by Matica Hrvatska in Čakovec.
* A permanent radio program in Kajkavian, ''Kajkavian Radio'' in Krapina. Other minor half-Kajkavian media with temporary Kajkavian contents include local television in Varaždin, the local radio program ''Sljeme'' in Zagreb, and some local newspapers in northwestern Croatia in Varaždin, Čakovec, Samobor, etc.
